description: Our team is composed of programmers, idea generators, members with knowledge of astronomy, and so on.
summary:
PlanetMatch is a web platform that finds and explains places on Earth that can serve as analogs for future bases and landing sites on the Moon and Mars. Users choose a test objective (rover navigation, astrobiology or base operations) and a target, such as Jezero Crater or the Artemis III lunar south pole. The platform then measures 20 Earth sites with the same criteria and ranks them using an explainable weighted distance.

It relies only on open data from NASA, ESA, JAXA and USGS: satellite terrain, climate, vegetation, soil, geology and the surface chemistry measured on Mars and the Moon. To keep the comparison fair, it compensates for scale and atmospheric differences between sensors and validates the ranking against known analogs such as Atacama and Haughton Crater.

Results include a map, 3D terrain and a scientific passport with sources, limitations and a proposed field experiment. The platform also surfaced a new candidate: Jalapão, Brazil, for rover testing. PlanetMatch helps teams choose where to test equipment based on evidence, not just on how a place looks.
details:
What it does and how it works

PlanetMatch finds, measures and explains places on Earth that can serve as analogs for future bases and landing sites on the Moon and Mars. It works in six steps. (1) Objective: the user picks a test objective - rover navigation, astrobiology or base operations - each with its own criteria and weights, each with a written rationale. (2) Target: the user picks a reference region, such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater or the Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole. (3) Search: the platform measures 20 Earth sites, both known references and less-studied regions, always over the same ground area and pixel size as the target. (4) Compare: an explainable weighted-distance ranking shows each criterion's calculation, the missing data and a validation against known analogs. (5) Explore: a map of the sites, side-by-side 3D terrain and satellite images, including Earth "seen" through the Mars or Moon camera. (6) Conclude: a scientific passport with evidence, sources, licenses, differences and a proposed field experiment.

Benefits

It replaces choosing by looks with choosing by reproducible measurements. It shows what is similar and also where the analogy fails: gravity, pressure, radiation and chemistry. It evaluates how real NASA hardware (Perseverance, VIPER and the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle) would perform on each terrain. Everything is open, free and runs in the browser, on desktop and mobile.

Intended impact

To help mission teams, researchers and students decide where to test rovers, instruments and operations before going to the Moon or Mars, and to surface new analogs. For example, the platform ranked Jalapão, Brazil, as the second closest site to Jezero for rover testing - a hypothesis that still requires field validation.

Tools, languages and software

Language: TypeScript throughout. Backend: Node.js with Express (MVC pattern). Frontend: React with Vite, three.js (3D terrain) and MapLibre (map). Data access: geotiff.js to read satellite file windows directly from the cloud. Hosting: Render. Data: NASA POWER, NASA MODIS, NASA PDS (Mars Odyssey and Lunar Prospector gamma-ray spectrometers), NASA GIBS and NASA Planetary Fact Sheets; MRO CTX (NASA/JPL) via USGS Astrogeology; ESA Copernicus DEM and Sentinel-2 via Microsoft Planetary Computer; JAXA Kaguya via USGS; ISRIC SoilGrids and Macrostrat. Hardware: no special equipment, only personal computers. AI: we used an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) to help with coding, review and documentation; all metrics and results come from the data, not from AI.

Creative aspect

An explainable index per objective instead of a single "percent similar to Mars"; terrain roughness compared across multiple scales; simulation of the Mars and Moon cameras using Sentinel-2 bands; pixel-by-pixel cloud removal; and a scientific passport for every site.

Factors the team considered

Scientific rigor: we compensate for scale and atmospheric differences between sensors, compare only relative measurements and never score missing data. Transparency: every criterion shows its rule, and we kept a failed validation visible (Death Valley) instead of tuning weights to pass. Trustworthy sources: 17 DOI-verified papers; sites without literature are labeled "proposed". Acknowledged limits: sensor resolution and the aspects Earth cannot reproduce. Zero cost, accessibility and reproducibility: open data and free hosting only, an interface for desktop and mobile, and a README, API routes and passports so the results can be reproduced.
